A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across appendix reordering and figure renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original repeated-run LLM experiments, intervention results, and metric-validation simulations. The human comparison data are attributed to earlier work.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds military-assignment, ReAct, socially salient demographic-label, and unequal-success experiments.

M1.justification: Appendix H adds a ReAct inference adaptation for GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash, replacing direct/CoT prompts with tool-mediated assignments and outcome observations. The original allocation procedure and diversity-steering intervention remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds military conscript assignment, hiring with familiar racial/ethnic labels and stereotype-linked occupations, and postgame identification of genuinely better-performing groups. Refugee resettlement was already evaluated in v1 and is not newly added coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix H adds ReAct as an evaluated alternative to the existing prompting approaches on the hiring task. The underlying model roster, human and random baselines, and four steering comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix J introduces group-dependent success probabilities of 0.90, 0.85, 0.80, and 0.75, compares explicitly announced 40- and 80-round horizons, and measures postgame group identification through independent queries sharing the completed interaction history. These are additional protocols; the original hiring experiments retain their settings.

E4.justification: New analyses examine agentic scaffolding, familiar versus artificial demographic labels, learning unequal success rates, and whether longer exploration improves identification. Figure 4 also adds a comparison with existing BBQ scores. Earlier feature ablations, prior-association checks, and diversity-versus-success analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C newly documents covariate adjustment and p < 0.001 for the previously collected human effect, explicitly attributing this analysis to Bai et al. The existing LLM repetition counts and 95% confidence-interval convention remain unchanged; additional result rows do not establish increased repetitions of earlier experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds military results, ReAct SIs of 1.11 and 1.42, real-label GASI values of 0.14–0.30, and best-group identification rates of 26.3% and 26.2% in the new 40- and 80-round tests. Original main plots and Tables 1–2 retain their results. The SI-validation curve changes, and the feature-ablation prose changes approximately 0.6 to 0.7 despite an unchanged corresponding plot.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1.1 adds a lemma and proof relating SI to mutual information under uniform job-category marginals. This is a bounded theoretical addition about an existing metric; the three original metric definitions remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and discussion retain the central claims about emergent biases, greater stratification in stronger models, and the effectiveness of explicit diversity incentives. The introduction mentions additional validation settings without redefining these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations that stratification persists without gamified rewards and under ReAct, that familiar demographic labels produce more prior-driven associations, and that longer interaction does not reliably uncover genuine performance differences. The earlier limitation concerning diversity rewards reducing success under true group differences is retained.

D1.justification: v2 supplies military-assignment prompts, the postgame identification prompt and context-handling details, and a description of the ReAct adaptation. Appendix C newly identifies the human baseline composition, including 200 participants per retained condition. These disclosures supplement the unchanged original prompts and model settings.

R1.justification: v2 removes the multi-turn-evaluation subsection and its six references, while adding He et al. on occupational stereotypes, Sørlie et al. on military selection, and Yao et al. on ReAct. The principal positioning around emergent bias and inadequate exploration remains intact.

P1.justification: Editing is localized: Section 5.2 expands, prompt explanations improve, appendices are reordered, and allocation matrices are grouped by model family. The multi-turn related-work subsection and acknowledgments are removed, but most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the BBQ comparison plot, a scenario-comparison plot, three result tables, and an illustrative allocation-matrix pair. It also substantially regroups and compacts the retained matrix displays and relocates metric analyses. The scenario plot partly redisplays existing resettlement evidence; most original graphics remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens targeted robustness and applicability evidence through Appendices H–J and makes the human comparison more transparent. These are useful, bounded extensions of an already multi-scenario study: several new checks cover only two models in simulated settings. The gains outweigh the loss of the brief multi-turn related-work discussion.
